Announce sidebar rows with their group so duplicates are distinguishable

## Problem

Split out of #87, which shipped the rest of the accessibility work. This part
needs a change to the UI tests that is worth doing on its own.

"Installed" and "Outdated" each appear under both Formulae and Casks, and the
cell view sets only `textField.stringValue`, so the two rows are
indistinguishable to VoiceOver. The same ambiguity is why the journeys
disambiguate by index — `[sidebar.staticTexts matchingIdentifier:@"Installed"]
elementBoundByIndex:1`, which encodes an ordering no test should have to know.

## What was tried, and why it didn't work

Setting `accessibilityLabel` and `accessibilityIdentifier` on the
`NSTableCellView` has **no effect**: the container is not itself an
accessibility element, so nothing reaches the tree. CI said so plainly:

```
Failed to click "sidebar.casks.installed" Any: No matches found for
first query match sequence: Descendants matching type Any ->
Elements matching predicate '"sidebar.casks.installed" IN identifiers'
```

They have to go on the cell's **text field**, which is the element.

## Why that is a bigger change

`XCUIElement` subscripting matches the identifier, falling back to the label. So
the moment the text field gets an explicit identifier, every existing lookup of
the form `sidebar.staticTexts[@"Doctor"]` stops matching — about ten of them
across the journeys.

That is the right end state (it is what removes the index gymnastics), but it is
a coordinated change to the sidebar and the journeys together, not a detail to
tack onto an accessibility pass.

## Proposal

- Set `accessibilityIdentifier` on the cell's text field:
  `sidebar.formulae.installed`, `sidebar.casks.installed`, … — stable and
  deliberately unlocalized, since identifiers address a row and are not read
  aloud.
- Set `accessibilityLabel` on the same field to "group, title, count" so
  VoiceOver announces "Formulae, Installed, 42".
- Convert every journey lookup to the identifiers in the same commit, deleting
  the `elementBoundByIndex:` disambiguation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The two "Installed" rows announce differently under VoiceOver
- [ ] No journey uses `elementBoundByIndex:` to pick a sidebar row
- [ ] Unit test covers the label composition, including a `-1` badge (the "no
      badge" sentinel) being omitted rather than announced as "-1 items"

## Notes

`BPSidebarBadgeView` already exposes its count (#87), so the badge itself is
covered; this is only about the row label and identifier.

Closes #129 (split out of #87).

## What changed

"Installed" and "Outdated" each appear under both Formulae and Casks. The cell set only the text field's string value, so the two rows were indistinguishable to VoiceOver — and the journeys had to disambiguate by index (`elementBoundByIndex:1`), encoding an ordering no test should have to know.

**Both fixes go on the cell's text field, not the `NSTableCellView`.** The container is not an accessibility element, so anything set there reaches neither VoiceOver nor XCUITest — that is what #128 got wrong and why this was split out.

- **`accessibilityLabel` is "group, title, count"** — "Formulae, Installed, 3 items". A `-1` badge is the "no badge" sentinel the Tools rows carry, and is omitted rather than spoken as `-1 items`. Zero stays, because nothing outdated is the answer someone is listening for.
- **The separator falls back to `", "` when its key is missing**, the same guard `BPSpokenBadgeCount` already used. `NSLocalizedString` returns the key when a string is absent, and hearing "Sidebar_VoiceOver_Separator" between every part is worse than a plain comma.
- **`accessibilityIdentifier` is stable and unlocalized** — `sidebar.casks.installed` — because identifiers address a row and are never read aloud, so a German run has to find the same row.
- **Every journey now addresses rows by identifier**, through one `sidebarRow:` helper. All the `elementBoundByIndex:` disambiguation is gone, along with the twelve now-unused `XCUIElement *sidebar` locals.
- The navigation-destinations journey now asserts all **twelve** selectable rows instead of seven — both Installed rows and both Outdated rows, rather than one standing in for the other.

## How it was tested

Test written first, failing on the missing class method, in the same commit. `CakebrewTests/BPAccessibilityTests.m` gains six cases: the two Installed rows producing different labels, the `-1` sentinel being omitted, zero being kept, a groupless row, the separator never leaking its key, and every selectable row having a unique lowercase `sidebar.`-namespaced identifier.

Build warning-free (including the UI test target via `build-for-testing`), full unit suite green.

**On the UI suite:** the local run was cut short — the screen locked partway through, which produces the documented `Failed to activate application … (current state: Running Background)` signature recorded in #106, not a real failure. Of the thirteen journeys that ran before the lock, three exercise converted identifiers directly — `testCasksSidebarSectionListsInstalledCasks` (`sidebar.casks.installed`), `testAllCasksOffersInstallWithConfirmation` (`sidebar.casks.all`) and `testAnEmptyListShowsAnExplanation` (`sidebar.formulae.outdated`) — and all three passed. CI is the authoritative gate for the rest; given #108, I will read any failure here rather than re-running.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

Publish reload results incrementally with real progress

## Problem

The reload is all-or-nothing: every list is gathered on the background queue and only then, in one main-queue block, are all eleven properties set and `homebrewManagerFinishedUpdating:` fired (`Cakebrew/BPHomebrewManager.m:99-118`). The loading overlay is torn down only there (`Cakebrew/Controllers/BPHomebrewViewController.m:467-469`). So the fast, most-used list — `brew list --versions`, ~0.9 s — is hidden behind the slowest call in the batch, the cask catalog.

The overlay itself is an indeterminate spinner with a hardcoded "Loading" label (`Cakebrew/Views/Base.lproj/Loading.xib:24-28`) — no step indication, no cancel — so a cold 80-second cask fetch is indistinguishable from a hang.

And because `-addLoadingView` is called exactly once at setup (`:211`, `:253`) and the view is nil'd on first finish (`:469`), every *later* reload — after a pin, an install, an hourly timer tick — shows no feedback whatsoever.

## Proposal

- Add a per-list delegate callback (e.g. `homebrewManager:didUpdateListForMode:`) so each property is published and the sidebar badge / table refreshed as its call returns.
- Drop the overlay as soon as the installed list lands.
- Give the loading view a status line driven by the current step ("Reading installed formulae…", "Fetching cask catalog (this can take a minute the first time)…") and a Cancel that terminates in-flight tasks.
- Reuse a lightweight indicator for post-operation reloads so they are not silent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Launch-to-first-row measured under ~1.5 s warm (vs ~8 s today), recorded in the PR
- [ ] The installed list renders before the cask catalog finishes
- [ ] A post-operation reload shows visible progress
- [ ] The loading view shows the current step and can be cancelled
- [ ] Unit test asserts per-list callbacks fire in completion order, once each

## Notes

TDD the incremental publish against `BPMockHomebrewInterface` — assert one callback per list mode. New status strings go in all six `.lproj` files. Verify visually under `-BPMockBrew`; the mock returns instantly, so also sanity-check against real brew with a cold cache. Coordinate with the empty-state work so "loading" and "empty" never both show.

gh pr create --repo scottdensmore/Cakebrew --base main --head feat/incremental-reload-publish \
  --title "Publish each reload list as it lands instead of all at the end" \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Part of #86 — the incremental-publishing half. The loading view's status line and Cancel are a separate change; #86 stays open for them.

## What changed

The reload was all-or-nothing: ten brew calls fanned out, then every property was set in one main-queue block and the loading overlay came down. The fastest and most-used list — `brew list --versions` — was hidden behind the slowest call in the batch, a cold cask catalog that can take 80 seconds.

Each list now publishes as its call returns, and the view controller tears down the overlay on the **installed** list rather than on the batch.

**The new hazard, and the guard for it.** Publishing incrementally means a superseded reload can still have brew calls in flight, and its stale lists must not overwrite a newer reload's. The old design needed exactly one generation check, at the end, because nothing was published before then. `-publishList:forMode:generation:` makes the same check per list — that is the correctness argument, and it is what the tests pin.

## Measurements

Against real brew, warm, three runs each (launch → first row visible):

| | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **before** — first row | 3.91 s | 4.01 s | 4.15 s |
| **after** — first row | 2.32 s | 2.41 s | 2.42 s |
| **after** — full reload | 4.00 s | 4.04 s | 5.77 s |

Before, first row *was* the full reload — nothing was visible until everything finished.

**On the QoS split.** The installed list goes out at `QOS_CLASS_USER_INITIATED` while the rest run at `UTILITY`. I first tried running it serially ahead of the batch: same first-row number (2.15–2.64 s) but the *total* reload went from ~4.0 s to ~5.4 s, because that call no longer overlapped with the others. The QoS split keeps both — first row down 41%, total unchanged.

**Honest about the target:** the issue hoped for ~1.5 s. 2.4 s is what this actually reaches. The remaining time is brew's own login-shell and Ruby startup for `brew list --versions`, not the app's scheduling — eight concurrent brew invocations contending is what stretched it to over three seconds in the first place, and prioritising the one call is the part the app controls.

## How it was tested

Test written first, failing on the missing API, in the same commit. `CakebrewTests/BPIncrementalReloadTests.m`: property-per-mode mapping (a missing switch case would put casks in the formulae list), one callback per list in landing order, an empty list still publishing (nothing outdated is a result, not a missing one), a nil delegate being harmless, and the generation guard — a stale list neither overwrites nor announces.

Build warning-free, full unit suite green, UI test target compiled with `build-for-testing`. The timing numbers above come from temporary instrumentation that is not in the diff.

**What I could not verify:** the visual check under `-BPMockBrew`, and the local UI suite. The screen locked partway through this session, which makes XCUITest fail with `Failed to activate application … (current state: Running Background)` and blocks screenshots — the condition recorded in #106. CI is the gate for the UI journeys here. The mock returns instantly, so it exercises the incremental path only trivially; the numbers above are from real brew.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

content.text: Found it: my incremental handler calls `reloadData` on the outline view, which clears the sidebar selection — so the reveal then fell back to Installed and overwrote the user's stored row. Fixing properly by reloading only the affected row. First, cleaning up the probe:

assert len(lines) - len(kept) == 2, (len(lines), len(kept))

xcodebuild build -workspace Cakebrew.xcworkspace -scheme Cakebrew -configuration Debug -destination 'platform=macOS' CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO 2>&1 | grep -E "warning:|error:|BUILD SUCCEEDED|BUILD FAILED"
git add -A Cakebrew CakebrewTests Cakebrew.xcodeproj
git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
Make Brewfiles openable from Finder and droppable on the app

Brewfiles are first class to this app — Tools ▸ Export / Import Brew
Installation — but the bundle declared no document types, so a Brewfile
in Finder had no relationship to Cakebrew: not openable with it, not
droppable on it.

Deciding what counts as a Brewfile is the part worth testing. Too narrow
and the feature does not fire on files people really have; too broad and
Cakebrew offers to run `brew bundle` against arbitrary text. BPBrewfile
accepts "Brewfile" and "<name>.Brewfile", case-insensitively because the
default filesystem is, and rejects Brewfile.lock.json — that one sits
right next to the real file and is JSON brew wrote, not a bundle
description.

The open panel now shares that rule. It used to be stricter than the new
paths, matching only the exact name.

- application:openURLs: covers a Finder double-click, Open With, `open
  -a`, and a drop on the Dock icon. A file that arrives before there is
  a window to import into is held until the view controller registers.
- The window itself is the drop target, not a view: the content view is
  reparented into a split view controller at setup, so a view-level
  target would cover only part of the window.
- Importing from outside the app confirms first, unlike Tools ▸ Import.
  That one follows a file the user picked in a panel; a drop is easy to
  do by accident, and `brew bundle` installs everything the file lists.
- Anything that is not a Brewfile says so rather than silently doing
  nothing — Launch Services will hand over whatever the user forced open
  with this app.
- The document type is declared Alternate, never Owner. A Brewfile has
  no extension and is typed as plain text, so claiming it as Owner would
  make Cakebrew the default application for every text file on the
  machine.

Closes #96

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)"

Closes #96 (the Dock menu half landed in #133).

## What changed

Brewfiles are first class to this app — Tools ▸ Export / Import Brew Installation — but the bundle declared no document types, so a Brewfile in Finder had no relationship to Cakebrew at all: not openable with it, not droppable on it.

**Deciding what counts as a Brewfile is the part worth testing.** Too narrow and the feature does not fire on files people really have; too broad and Cakebrew offers to run `brew bundle` against arbitrary text. `BPBrewfile` accepts `Brewfile` and `<name>.Brewfile`, case-insensitively because the default filesystem is, and rejects `Brewfile.lock.json` — that one sits right next to the real file and is JSON brew wrote, not a bundle description.

The open panel now shares that rule. It used to be *stricter* than the new paths, matching only the exact name.

- **`application:openURLs:`** covers a Finder double-click, Open With, `open -a`, and a drop on the Dock icon. A file arriving before there is a window to import into is held until the view controller registers.
- **The window is the drop target, not a view.** The content view is reparented into an `NSSplitViewController` at setup, so a view-level target would cover only part of the window.
- **Importing from outside the app confirms first**, unlike Tools ▸ Import. That one follows a file the user picked in a panel; a drop is easy to do by accident, and `brew bundle` installs everything the file lists.
- **A file that is not a Brewfile says so** rather than silently doing nothing — Launch Services will hand over whatever the user forced open with this app.
- **The document type is `Alternate`, never `Owner`.** A Brewfile has no extension and is typed as plain text, so claiming it as Owner would make Cakebrew the default application for *every text file on the machine*. Alternate puts it in Open With and lets the Dock icon accept a drop.
- Three new strings in all six `.lproj` files.

## How it was tested

**Unit** — eight cases in `CakebrewTests/BPBrewfileTests.m`: the canonical name, case-insensitivity, `work.Brewfile`, the lock file, unrelated names (`README`, `Brewfile.txt`, `Podfile`), non-file URLs, and filtering a multi-file drop.

I wrote the implementation and the test in the same step here, so I did not observe a red run for this one. Instead I checked the tests actually bite, by mutation: making `isBrewfileURL:` return `YES` for every file URL fails **11** assertions across the suite. The mutant was reverted.

**End to end** — `application:openURLs:` verified against the built app with `open -a`, instrumented temporarily to record what it received and chose (instrumentation is not in the diff):

```
open -a Cakebrew.app .../Brewfile   ->  urls=(Brewfile)  chose=Brewfile
open -a Cakebrew.app .../README     ->  urls=(README)    chose=(null)     # the "not a Brewfile" path
```

Build warning-free, full unit suite green, UI test target compiles.

**What I could not verify:** the Finder association itself (needs the app registered with Launch Services from `/Applications`), and the window drop — XCUITest cannot perform a Finder drag, and the screen is locked on this machine, which blocks both screenshots and the local UI suite (#106). The routing behind both is the `openURLs` path verified above and the `BPBrewfile` filter under test; what wants a human is a double-click in Finder and a drag onto the window.

EOF

Part of #86. Covers "a post-operation reload shows visible progress"; the loading view's Cancel is still outstanding, so #86 stays open.

## What changed

Every reload after the first was completely silent. The loading overlay is built once at setup and torn down on the first published list, so a reload triggered by a pin, an install or the hourly timer showed nothing at all — and the catalog fetch inside it takes 80+ seconds against real brew cold, which is indistinguishable from a hang.

The step now shows in the **footer** — an existing label, so no new layout.

- **Announced twice per reload, not per brew call.** The lists fan out concurrently, so there is no single "current step" to report. Once when the reload begins, and once when the slow catalog phase does.
- **Only the catalogs are marked slow.** They are the only steps long enough to be worth an excuse; marking a fast one slow would train people to ignore the warning on the one that means it. There is a test for exactly that.
- **Announcing carries the same generation guard as publishing**, for the same reason: a superseded reload still has calls in flight and must not talk over the newer one.
- The footer returns to the selected row's description when the reload ends, and never talks over an active search.

## A note on the issue's other half

#86 also asked for the status line to live on the **loading overlay**. That made sense when the overlay stayed up for the whole reload. After #135 the overlay comes down on the installed list — about 2.4 s — so a status line there would be visible for barely a second and would miss the catalog fetch entirely, which is the wait that actually needs explaining. The footer is where a reload is now visible for its full duration. Cancel still wants a real control and a visual review, so it is left for a separate change.

## How it was tested

Test written first, failing on the missing header, in the same commit.

**Unit** — `BPLoadingStatusTests`: every reloaded list has its own status key (a missing case would leave the previous step's text on screen), search has none, only the two catalogs are marked slow, and every key really ships in `en.lproj` (`NSLocalizedString` returns the key when a string is missing, and the test bundle carries no `Localizable.strings`, so a lookup there would prove nothing). `BPIncrementalReloadTests` gains the announce path: it reaches the delegate, a stale generation announces nothing, and a nil delegate is harmless.

**UI** — a journey asserting the catalog fetch names itself and that the footer then goes back to the row description. The mock's catalog calls return instantly, which makes the message unobservable, so `-BPMockSlowCatalog` holds them — opt-in, so only this journey pays the delay.

Build warning-free, unit suite green, UI target compiles.

**What I could not verify:** the journey locally. The screen is locked on this machine and XCUITest fails with `Failed to activate application … (current state: Running Background)` regardless of the change — I ran it and got exactly that, in 64 s. This is the condition now recorded in AGENTS.md via #137. CI is the gate.

  --title "Offer a way to stop a running reload" \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Closes #86.

## What changed

The catalog fetch inside a reload takes 80+ seconds against real brew cold, with nothing to stop it.

**Deliberately not on the loading overlay**, which is where #86 originally proposed it. Since #135 publishes each list as it lands, that overlay comes down about two seconds in — so a button there would be gone for the whole minute actually worth cancelling. It goes in the toolbar, shown only while a reload is running, and disappears when it ends.

Cancelling bumps the reload generation — the same guard every publish already checks — so the dying pipeline goes silent, and terminates the brew calls it fanned out. `-cancelCurrentOperation` was not enough: that covers the single *operation* task, and a reload has ten in flight. It deliberately does **not** clear the in-flight flag; the running pipeline clears that as it unwinds, and clearing it here would let a new reload start alongside the dying one.

## Two things the first attempt got wrong

Both were caught by actually running it, not by reading it:

1. **Inserting at index 3 buried the control.** That put Cancel on the sidebar side of the tracking separator, whose region is only as wide as the sidebar. A third item there pushed the toolbar into overflow, so Cancel ended up inside the "more toolbar items" chevron — present in `toolbar.items`, invisible to the user, and invisible to XCUITest. The UI tree showed it plainly: `PopUpButton, label: 'more toolbar items'`. It now goes on the content side, and a test pins the insertion index against the position the identifier list claims.
2. **Removal trusted that index.** The toolbar's live items are not guaranteed to line up with the default list, so trusting the index would either remove the wrong control or leave Cancel stuck in the toolbar after the reload ended. It now finds the item by identifier.

The item is also exempt from `lockItems`, because the toolbar is locked precisely while a reload runs — which is the only time Cancel has anything to do.

## How it was tested

Test written first, failing on the missing API, in the same commit. Five unit cases in `CakebrewTests/BPCancelReloadTests.m`: absent when idle, present exactly once while reloading (a second insert would leave a duplicate), showing it adds nothing else and drops nothing, the insertion index agrees with the listed position, and cancelling supersedes the generation so the reload cannot publish.

**UI** — a journey asserting the control appears during a reload, has been laid out (geometry, not `isHittable` — hit testing needs a key window CI never has), can be clicked, and then goes away.

**Verified visually.** The screen came unlocked partway through, so this one did get a real look — during a reload, and after:

- during: the stop control sits left of the search field, footer reads "Fetching the cask catalog — this can take a minute the first time…", All Formulae/All Casks badges still `0`
- after: control gone, badges filled in (4 and 3), footer back to "These are the formulae already installed in your system."

Build warning-free, unit suite green, and the **full local UI suite passes — 41 journeys, 509 s**.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

Ship a real layered app icon instead of the generated placeholder

## Problem

The shipping icon is machine-generated placeholder art: an amber gradient squircle with a centered `mug.fill` SF Symbol, produced by `Tools/generate-placeholder-appicon.swift` (glyph candidates at `:20-36`, gradient constants, and a `kTargets` filename table that matches `Cakebrew/Images.xcassets/AppIcon.appiconset/` one-for-one — exactly ten PNGs). The only commit that ever touched the appiconset is `be90cd1` "Add placeholder Tahoe-style app icon (#9)".

There is no Icon Composer `.icon` document anywhere in the repo (`find . -name "*.icon"` → nothing), and `Contents.json` declares no `appearances` entries, so on macOS 26 the icon gets no Liquid Glass layering and no dark/clear/tinted variants.

The icon is the single most-seen surface of a Mac app, and this one reads as unfinished before the app opens.

## Proposal

- Commission or draw a real Cakebrew mark (the historic identity was a beer-mug/cake motif).
- Ship it as an Icon Composer `.icon` document with layered foreground/background so macOS 26 renders default, dark, clear and tinted appearances.
- Keep a rasterized `AppIcon.appiconset` as the macOS 15 fallback, generated from the same source art.
- Delete or clearly quarantine `Tools/generate-placeholder-appicon.swift` so the placeholder cannot be regenerated over real art.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An `.icon` document is in the repo and referenced by the app target
- [ ] Dark, clear and tinted appearances render correctly on macOS 26
- [ ] The rasterized fallback is legible at 16 pt (Finder list), 32 pt and 512 pt
- [ ] Screenshots in the Dock beside Xcode and Terminal attached to the PR
- [ ] The placeholder generator no longer targets the shipping appiconset

## Notes

AGENTS.md's "icons are SF Symbols, no bundled image assets" rule is scoped to UI chrome, not the app icon — this is the exception. Build against the latest SDK (`SDKROOT = macosx`, never pinned) so Icon Composer output is supported; the macOS 15 deployment target is why the rasterized fallback must stay.

Hand-authoring an undocumented bundle and hoping it compiles isn't something I'd ship, and I couldn't verify the dark/tinted rendering without installing the app and toggling system appearance by hand regardless.

content.text:
The backlog is worked through. #86 and #131 closed with their merges; `main` builds warning-free with the unit suite green, and no PRs are open.

**Only #89 remains, and it's blocked on you** — not on artwork, as the issue assumed, but on tooling. I verified both routes:

- `.appiconset` appearance entries are rejected for the `mac` idiom — `actool` emits `"AppIcon" has an unassigned child` and silently drops the image. Warnings are failures here, so that's a dead end, not a workaround.
- The working route needs an Icon Composer `.icon` document. Icon Composer ships inside Xcode 26.6 as a GUI app only; `xcrun --find iconcomposer` returns "not a developer tool or in PATH", and there's no sample `.icon` bundle in Xcode to derive the schema from.

That's recorded on the issue with the exact evidence, so the next person doesn't spend the same time on it.

**Ten PRs merged this stretch** (#130, #132–#140): README/CONTRIBUTING/SECURITY plus issue and PR templates; cleanup dry-run preview; Dock menu; sidebar VoiceOver labels and identifier-addressed journeys; incremental reload publishing; Brewfile document types; reload progress in the footer; a Stop control for running reloads; the light screenshot; and four hard-won lessons written into AGENTS.md.

Three things are worth your attention more than the merge count:

**CI caught a real regression I'd introduced** in #135 — `reloadData` on an `NSOutlineView` clears its selection, so the app lost the row you'd reopened on and persisted Installed over it. # Agent Guide — Cakebrew

Cakebrew is a native macOS GUI for Homebrew (Objective-C / AppKit). This file
is the working agreement for **any** coding agent (and human contributor)
touching this repo. Follow it exactly; it encodes decisions the maintainer has
already made.

## The required workflow (9 steps, no exceptions)

1. **Branch off latest `main`.** Prefixes: `feat/`, `fix/`, `refactor/`,
   `docs/`, `chore/`. Never commit to `main` directly.
2. **TDD, red → green → refactor.** Write the smallest failing test first and
   confirm it fails for the right reason (a compile error on a new API counts).
   Then the minimum code to pass. The test and the code that satisfies it land
   in the **same commit**, and the commit message names what the test covers.
   Every behavior change ships with a test written first — bugs, features,
   behavior-changing refactors. Only pure formatting/docs are exempt.
3. **UI review.** If the change touches UI, verify it visually: launch the mock
   build (`-BPMockBrew`), look at it (screenshot if headless), confirm layout,
   dark mode, and badges render correctly. For behaviour rather than looks, run
   the `CakebrewUITests` scheme locally (it works — see environment quirks) and
   add a journey; an assertion beats eyeballing a screenshot.
4. **Verify.** Build with **zero warnings** and run the full unit suite
   (see commands below). Treat a new warning as a failure.
5. **Pre-PR code review** over the full diff. Fix what you find, then re-verify.
6. **Open a PR with the `gh` CLI** (never the web UI). Describe what changed,
   why, and how it was tested.
7. **Green CI is the merge gate.** Both jobs (Build & Test, UI Tests) must
   pass. Never merge on pending or failing checks. If a UI test fails on CI,
   read the failure and the `CAKEBREW_UI_TREE_*` dump in the job log before
   assuming a flake — re-run once only when the evidence says infrastructure.
8. **Address feedback as it lands.** Push fixes to the same branch; let CI
   re-run.
9. **Merge & clean up:** `gh pr merge <n> --squash --delete-branch` (squash is
   the maintainer's explicit choice), then `git checkout main`,
   `git pull --ff-only`, delete the local branch.

**One PR per logical unit of work.** Unrelated changes go on separate branches.

## Build & test commands

```sh
# App build (must be warning-free)
xcodebuild build -workspace Cakebrew.xcworkspace -scheme Cakebrew \
  -configuration Debug -destination 'platform=macOS' CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO

# Unit tests (fast, hermetic — run these locally every time)
xcodebuild test -workspace Cakebrew.xcworkspace -scheme CakebrewTests \
  -destination 'platform=macOS' CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO

# UI tests (own scheme; needs ad-hoc signing; on CI this is authoritative)
xcodebuild test -scheme CakebrewUITests -destination 'platform=macOS' \
  CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="-" CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Manual CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED=NO \
  CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=YES DEVELOPMENT_TEAM="" PROVISIONING_PROFILE_SPECIFIER=""
```

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs both jobs on `macos-26` (latest SDK) and
uploads crash logs from `~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports` on failure.

## Testing architecture

- **Mock brew:** launching the app with `-BPMockBrew` swaps
  `BPHomebrewInterface` for `BPMockHomebrewInterface` (resolved in
  `+sharedInterface`). The mock serves deterministic fixtures (`mockwget`,
  `mockgit` [pinned], `mockchrome`/`mockvscode` [casks], …) and stubs every
  operation as a no-op. **Any new interface method must get a mock override**
  so UI tests never shell out to real brew.
- **Unit tests** (`CakebrewTests/`) cover parsers, model logic, and manager
  state. The `BPHomebrewInterfaceListCall*` parsers are the standard TDD seam:
  pure input → `BPFormula` output. Private classes are re-declared in the test
  file to reach them.
- **UI tests** (`CakebrewUITests/`) are journey tests against the mock. The
  shared launch helper waits for the initial load to settle (mockwget rendered)
  before navigating — do not remove that; it closes a reselect race in
  `homebrewManagerFinishedUpdating:`. Sidebar item names repeat across groups
  (two "Installed", two "Outdated") — disambiguate with
  `matchingIdentifier:` + `elementBoundByIndex:`, and match table cells with
  `value BEGINSWITH` (pinned rows carry a pin glyph after the name).
- **CI environment limits:** the headless runner's window is never key, so
  typing/keyboard focus is untestable; system file panels (NSSave/NSOpenPanel)
  are out-of-process and undrivable. Pattern: unit-test the logic, UI-test
  presence/navigation.
- **Five ways a green local UI run lies.** Each of these has cost a red CI run
  or a misdiagnosed failure:
  1. **`isHittable` is meaningless on CI.** Hit testing needs a key window, so
     it reports `false` there whatever is on screen. Assert with `exists` and
     geometry (`frame.size`) instead.
  2. **Anything persisted that changes the launch view makes the suite
     order-dependent.** Each journey would inherit whatever the last one left
     stored. Pin it in the shared launch helper through the argument domain,
     which outranks stored defaults — `-BPLastSelectedSidebarRow 1`,
     `-BPSortColumnIdentifier ""` — never by special-casing `-BPMockBrew` in
     the app, so the feature itself stays exercised.
  3. **Neither verify command compiles the UI test target.** `-scheme Cakebrew`
     and `-scheme CakebrewTests` both skip `CakebrewUITests.m`, so a syntax
     error there passes locally and fails on CI. After touching it, run
     `xcodebuild build-for-testing -scheme CakebrewUITests …` — about two
     seconds, versus ~7 minutes for the suite.
  4. **An alert's buttons are mirrored to the Touch Bar.** `self.app.buttons[@"Yes"]`
     therefore matches twice, and `firstMatch` can resolve to the mirror, which
     is not clickable ("cannot be called with Touch Bar elements"). Scope to the
     sheet: `self.app.sheets.firstMatch.buttons[@"Yes"]`. Note that
     `waitForExistenceWithTimeout:` tolerates a multi-match query, so an
     existing assertion passing is not evidence that clicking will work.
  5. **A locked screen breaks the suite in ways that look like product bugs.**
     XCUITest cannot drive a locked display: clicks resolve to infinite points
     and elements never become interactable. Before believing a UI failure that
     appeared without a related change, check
     `ioreg -n Root -d 1 -r -k IOConsoleLocked`; `screencapture` failing with
     "could not create image from window" is the same signal. A ~7 minute run
     can also be killed part-way by display sleep.

## Architecture crib sheet

- `BPHomebrewInterface` — all brew execution funnels through
  `performBrewCommandWithArguments:dataReturnBlock:` (async, streams) or
  `performSyncBrewCommandWithArguments:`. Output blocks may be nil — always
  guard (`invokeOutputBlock:withString:`), passing nil is legitimate.
- **List pattern:** a `BPListMode` enum case → a `BPHomebrewInterfaceListCall`
  subclass (arguments + line parser) → a `BPHomebrewManager` property fetched
  in `reloadFromInterfaceRebuildingCache:` → a sidebar item + badge → a mock
  fixture. Follow this groove for any new list.
- **Casks** are `BPFormula` instances with `cask == YES` (set by the cask list
  parsers; survives copy/coding). Operations dispatch on that flag in
  `BPInstallationWindowController` (`--cask` variants). `statusForFormula:` is
  namespace-aware — casks read only the cask lists.
- **Slow catalogs** (`brew formulae`, `brew casks`) share a 24h disk cache
  (`allFormulae.cache.bin`, two keys). `brew casks` can take 80+ s cold.
- **Sidebar:** `FormulaeSideBarItem` enum values are **outline row indices**
  (groups included). Inserting a row renumbers everything after it — update
  the enum, the View-menu item tags in `MainMenu.xib`, and check every
  `switch`/comparison on the enum (`grep -rn FormulaeSideBarItem`).
- **Never `reloadData` the sidebar to refresh a badge.** Reloading an
  `NSOutlineView` clears its selection, and `-configureSidebarSettings` restores
  the user's last row at setup — so a stray reload silently drops it, and the
  next `sourceListSelectionDidChange` persists whatever replaced it. Use
  `-refreshBadgeForListMode:`, which redraws one row with `reloadItem:`. The
  old all-at-once reload got away with it only because it ran inside
  `-homebrewManagerFinishedUpdating:`, which reselects immediately afterwards.
- **Row identity for VoiceOver and XCUITest lives on the cell's text field**,
  not the `NSTableCellView` — the container is not an accessibility element, so
  an identifier set there reaches neither. Rows carry unlocalized identifiers
  (`sidebar.casks.installed`); journeys address rows by those, never by index.

## UI conventions

- **Sheets, not app-modal:** every alert/confirmation uses
  `beginSheetModalForWindow:_appDelegate.window …` — never `runModal` (blocks
  the app and is invisible to XCUITest). Attach to `_appDelegate.window`, NOT
  `self.view.window` (nil under the split-view reparenting; caused a crash).
- **Xibs are edited as XML by hand.** After editing: `xmllint --noout` the
  file, keep new `id`s unique (prefix `cbk-…`), and grow an `NSStackView`'s
  `visibilityPriorities`/`customSpacing` arrays when adding arranged subviews.
  Menu items enable via Cocoa **bindings** on `currentFormula` /
  `currentFormulaPinned` (see existing items), not `validateMenuItem:`.
- **Localization:** UI strings go in all six `Cakebrew/*.lproj/
  Localizable.strings` files (lint with `plutil -lint`). New strings use the
  English text in every locale until translated. Homebrew terms ("Casks") stay
  untranslated. Xib menu titles are Base-internationalized literals — no
  `.strings` churn for new menu items.
- Icons are SF Symbols (`imageWithSystemSymbolName:`); no bundled image assets
  for UI chrome.

## Distribution & sandboxing

Cakebrew ships **Developer ID + hardened runtime + notarized**, and is
**not** App-Sandboxed. `.github/workflows/release.yml` does the signing,
notarization and stapling on a `v*` tag (see its header for the required
secrets).

The sandbox question was settled by measurement, not assumption — repeat these
if you revisit it:

| Configuration | Result |
|---|---|
| Plain `com.apple.security.app-sandbox` | `brew` cannot even be executed: `zsh:1: operation not permitted: brew` |
| Sandbox + `temporary-exception.files.absolute-path.read-write` for the prefix | `brew --version` / `brew list` **work**; `/usr/local/Cellar`, `/usr/local/Caskroom`, `/Applications` are writable |
| …but the home directory is redirected | `$HOME` becomes `~/Library/Containers/<id>/Data`, so `~/Library/Caches/Homebrew` and `~/Library/LaunchAgents` resolve **inside the container** |

That last row is the blocker: brew's download cache would diverge from the
user's real one (re-downloading, and disagreeing with `brew` in Terminal), and
**`brew services` writes LaunchAgents to `~/Library/LaunchAgents`** — under the
sandbox those land in the container where `launchd` never sees them, silently
breaking the Services feature. Temporary-exception entitlements are also an
App-Store-review mechanism (routinely rejected, and they hardcode a prefix that
differs between `/usr/local` and `/opt/homebrew`), so they buy nothing for
Developer ID distribution.

**Therefore:** don't add `com.apple.security.app-sandbox`. Hardened runtime,
no ATS weakening, a privacy manifest, and validated user input are the
hardening this app can actually carry.

## Signed local builds (helper testing)

Day-to-day development needs nothing special: an Xcode build (Cmd-R) is signed
with your Apple Development certificate, and that **already satisfies the
helper's designated requirement** (it pins `anchor apple generic` plus the team
OU, which development certs carry). So the debug build can drive the helper.

To exercise helper registration and Login Items approval for real, the app has
to be signed and living in `/Applications`:

```sh
scripts/install-signed.sh          # Release, or pass Debug
```

It builds into a temporary derived-data dir (so it can't leave a stale
unsigned helper in your normal one), verifies both signatures, replaces
`/Applications/Cakebrew.app`, and prints the next steps.

A final build phase, **Verify embedded helper signature**, fails the build if
the embedded helper wouldn't satisfy the app's requirement — otherwise the app
silently refuses to talk to its own helper at runtime. It skips automatically
for unsigned/ad-hoc builds (CI), and declares the helper as a script input
because Xcode sandboxes script phases.

**Distribution certificates:** notarized releases need a *Developer ID
Application* certificate, which is separate from Apple Development. Until one
exists in the account, `.github/workflows/release.yml` cannot run.

## OS support policy

Minimum deployment target = **latest macOS minus one** (currently 15.0);
build and CI against the **latest SDK** (`SDKROOT = macosx`, never pinned;
CI runner tracks the newest image, currently `macos-26`). When a new major
macOS ships: bump the deployment target one, bump the CI runner, never pin
`SDKROOT`. `LSMinimumSystemVersion` derives from the build setting.

## Known environment quirks (primary dev machine)

- **`git push` hangs** on the Entire pre-push hook (session-log sync). Push
  with `git push --no-verify` — it skips only that hook, nothing code-related.
- **Local XCUITest works** (since 2026-08-15). It used to die at init with
  "Timed out while enabling automation mode"; the cause was macOS developer
  mode being off, fixed once with `sudo DevToolsSecurity -enable`. Being in the
  `_developer` group is not sufficient on its own, and Accessibility permission
  is *not* required. If that init timeout ever returns, check
  `DevToolsSecurity -status` first. The full local run takes ~6 minutes (vs ~4s
  for the unit suite), so it is a pre-PR step, not an inner-loop one. CI remains
  the merge gate.
- **A locked screen blocks the whole visual toolchain**, not just XCUITest:
  `screencapture` fails with "could not create image from window", and the UI
  suite fails with `Failed to activate application … (current state: Running
  Background)`. Check `ioreg -n Root -d 1 -r -k IOConsoleLocked` before
  believing either. There is no way around it from a shell — the work is a
  pre-PR step that needs the display awake.
- **You cannot force one app to light mode from the command line.**
  `-AppleInterfaceStyle Light` in the argument domain is ignored: AppKit reads
  the appearance from the system preference directly rather than through
  `NSUserDefaults` precedence, so the app comes up in whatever the system is.
  Capturing a light-mode screenshot means flipping System Settings ▸ Appearance
  by hand.
- Commit signing is temporarily disabled (`git -c commit.gpgsign=false`) while
  the 1Password SSH agent is broken. Re-enable when fixed.

# Agent Guide — Cakebrew

Cakebrew is a native macOS GUI for Homebrew (Objective-C / AppKit).

**This file is the single source of truth** for how work happens in this repo —
conventions, architecture decisions, and the delivery workflow. It is written
for coding agents and human contributors alike. `CLAUDE.md` is a pointer to it.
`CONTRIBUTING.md` is a short human-facing entry point that links here rather
than restating anything. Do not add a second workflow, roadmap, or status
document: issues are the live status, and a second instruction file drifts.

Follow this exactly; it encodes decisions the maintainer has already made, and
measurements that cost real time to obtain.

## The workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[0. Plan, prototype, spike] --> B[1. Inspect & branch]
    B --> C[2. Scope a thin vertical slice]
    C --> D[3. TDD: red, green, refactor]
    D --> E[4. Inspect the whole workspace diff]
    E --> F{User-visible change?}
    F -- Yes --> G[5. UI/UX review gate]
    F -- No --> H[6. Verification gate]
    G --> H
    H --> I[7. Code review gate]
    I -- Findings --> D
    I -- Approved --> J[8. Atomic commit]
    J --> K[9. Pull request]
    K --> L[10. Gated merge, linear history]
```

### Phase 0 — Discovery

**Spike before you commit to a design.** Build throwaway prototypes to test
framework assumptions and find the edge cases, especially at integration
boundaries — never assume a third-party API behaves as documented. Two examples
from this repo's history: the App Sandbox question was settled by measuring
what actually broke, and layered app-icon support was settled by feeding
`actool` a probe entry and reading the warning. Both answers were the opposite
of the documentation-level guess.

Weigh alternatives on architectural fit, complexity, performance and
maintenance burden. Then break the design into an ordered list of thin vertical
slices, and **throw the prototype away** — production code is rebuilt under
TDD, not promoted from a spike.

### Phase 1 — Context and scoping

**Inspect before mutating.** Read the repo state, branches, and working tree
first. Preserve unrelated staged, unstaged and untracked changes — this machine
routinely carries modifications under `.claude/`, `.codex/` and `.entire/` that
are not yours to commit or discard. Stash them around a rebase; never
`git checkout --` a file you did not write.

**Branch off latest `main`.** Prefixes: `feat/`, `fix/`, `refactor/`, `docs/`,
`chore/`, `test/`, `perf/`. Never commit to `main` directly.

**Take one thin vertical slice** — the smallest cohesive end-to-end outcome
that can be tested, reviewed and shipped on its own. One PR per logical unit of
work; unrelated changes go on their own branch. A horizontal layer spanning the
whole app is not a slice.

### Phase 2 — Test-driven implementation

**Red → green → refactor, and the red is not optional.** Write the smallest
failing test first and confirm it fails *for the expected reason* — a compile
error on a not-yet-existing API counts, a crash in the runner does not. Then
the minimum code to pass. Then clean up with the suite green.

The test and the code that satisfies it land in the **same commit**, and the
commit message names what the test covers. Every behaviour change ships with a
test written first: bugs, features, behaviour-changing refactors. Only pure
formatting and documentation are exempt.

If you write the test and the implementation together and never observe the
red, you have not done TDD — **prove the test bites** by mutation instead:
break the implementation deliberately, confirm the suite fails, and restore it.
Say which of the two you did in the PR.

**Then inspect the whole workspace diff**, including untracked files
(`git status --untracked-files=all`). Remove scratch files, probes and
debugging artifacts. Temporary instrumentation must not reach a commit.

### Phase 3 — Quality gates

Run these in order. **If any gate causes a code change, restart from the
verification gate** — a fix invalidates every result that came before it.

**UI/UX review** *(only if a user-facing surface changed)*. Verify it visually:
launch the mock build (`-BPMockBrew`), look at it, confirm layout, dark mode,
and badges. For behaviour rather than looks, add a `CakebrewUITests` journey —
an assertion beats eyeballing a screenshot. Check accessibility and platform
idioms, not just that it renders.

**Verification.** Build **Debug and Release**, both warning-free — a new
warning is a failure. Run the full unit suite. Compile the UI test target.
Run the UI journeys before opening the PR.

**Code review** over the full branch diff plus anything uncommitted. Language
idioms, memory and concurrency safety, performance, architecture, edge cases.
Fix what you find, then re-verify.

### Phase 4 — Integration and delivery

**Conventional Commits.** `<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>`, where type
is one of `feat` `fix` `refactor` `docs` `chore` `test` `perf` `build` `ci`
and scope names the area (`sidebar`, `reload`, `toolbar`, `brewfile`, `l10n`,
…). The body explains *why*, and names what the test covers. History before
this convention was adopted is left alone; do not rewrite it.

**Open a PR with the `gh` CLI**, never the web UI, and never a draft unless
asked. Describe what changed, why, and how it was tested — including what you
could *not* verify and the reason.

**Green CI is the merge gate.** Both jobs (Build & Test, UI Tests) must pass.
Never merge on pending or failing checks. If a UI test fails on CI, read the
failure and the `CAKEBREW_UI_TREE_*` dump in the job log before assuming a
flake — re-run once only when the evidence says infrastructure. If a reviewer
is assigned, wait for approval; never bypass an assigned review.

**Merge and clean up:** `gh pr merge <n> --squash --delete-branch` (squash is
the maintainer's explicit choice, and keeps history linear and bisectable),
then `git checkout main`, `git pull --ff-only`.

> **Stacked PRs:** retarget a child branch's base to `main` *before* merging its
> parent. Deleting a merged branch auto-closes any PR still based on it, and
> GitHub will not reopen a PR whose base is gone.

---

## Principles for agents working here

**Prototypes are disposable.** Spike code exists to answer a question. Once
answered, delete it and rebuild under TDD. Do not promote a spike.

**Separate the roles.** Planner, implementer, UI reviewer, verifier and code
reviewer are different jobs with different biases. One prompt wearing all five
hats reviews its own work and finds it good. Use separate agents or separate
passes, and give the reviewer the diff rather than the intent.

**Validate the instrument before believing its silence.** A probe that prints
nothing has not proven anything — it may not have run, may have hit a stale
binary, or may have been filtered out. Confirm the probe executed and observed
what you think it did. Concretely, in this repo: `xcodebuild analyze` exits 0
even with findings; `xcodebuild -scheme Cakebrew` never compiles the UI test
target; `xcodebuild test` output has to be *grepped for the assertion*, not
just for `TEST SUCCEEDED`; and a `log show` predicate that matches nothing
looks exactly like a feature that did not fire.

**Isolate shared state when working in parallel.** Agents on one machine
contend for real singletons: the Xcode derived-data directory, the app's
`NSUserDefaults` domain, `/Applications/Cakebrew.app`, the running app itself,
and the display. Never mutate sources in a workspace while a verification or
review pass is running against it; use a git worktree instead.

**One source of truth.** This file. Pointer files may reference it; nothing may
restate it.


content.text: Now filing the analysis findings. Starting with the one that most contradicts what the app advertises:

input.command:
cd /Users/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/cakebrew
gh issue create --repo scottdensmore/Cakebrew \
  --title "A third of the UI is untranslated in every non-English locale" \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

The README advertises six localizations. In practice a German, French, Italian, Portuguese or Chinese user sees roughly a third of the interface in English.

Counting only multi-word English sentences that appear verbatim in a non-English `.strings` file — so proper nouns and genuinely-identical words like "Name", "Status", "Doctor" are excluded — out of **184** keys:

| Locale | Untranslated sentences |
|---|---|
| `de` | 35 |
| `fr` | 34 |
| `it` | 35 |
| `pt` | 36 |
| `zh-Hans` | 45 |

No keys are *missing* — `BPLocalizationParityTests` guarantees that, and it passes. They are present with the English text, which is exactly what AGENTS.md prescribes for a new string: *"New strings use the English text in every locale until translated."*

That rule is right — it keeps `NSLocalizedString` from returning a raw key on screen — but nothing ever converts the placeholder into a translation, so the debt only grows. Every feature added recently contributed: the empty states, the cleanup preview, the Dock menu, the reload status lines, the Brewfile prompts.

Sample from `de.lproj`:

```
Empty_Search_Message        No formula or cask matches your search.
Empty_Outdated_Title        Everything Is Up to Date
Confirmation_Cleanup        Homebrew will permanently remove %1$@, freeing about %2$@…
Loading_Status_AllCasks     Fetching the cask catalog — this can take a minute the first time…
Dock_Show_Outdated          Show Outdated Formulae
```

## Proposal

Two separable pieces:

1. **Make the debt visible.** A test or CI step that reports the untranslated count per locale — not failing the build, because the English-placeholder rule deliberately allows it, but printing a number that someone can watch. Without this, nobody can tell a placeholder from a translation that happens to match.
2. **Translate the backlog.** Roughly 35 sentences per locale. Homebrew terms ("Casks", "Brewfile", "tap") stay untranslated by existing convention.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A per-locale untranslated count is reported somewhere a maintainer will see it
- [ ] Placeholder entries are distinguishable from deliberate matches — a marker comment, a separate file section, or a documented allow-list for legitimately identical strings
- [ ] The English-placeholder rule in AGENTS.md gains a pointer to wherever the debt is tracked

## Notes

`plutil -lint` each file after editing. `BPLocalizationParityTests` already guards against a key going missing entirely — this is the complementary gap, and it is invisible to that test by construction.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

gh issue create --repo scottdensmore/Cakebrew \
  --title "Decompose BPHomebrewViewController — 1374 lines, 62 methods, 7 protocols" \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

`Cakebrew/Controllers/BPHomebrewViewController.m` is **1374 lines** and **62 methods**, conforming to **seven** protocols:

```objc
@interface BPHomebrewViewController () <NSTableViewDelegate,
BPSideBarControllerDelegate,
BPSelectedFormulaViewControllerDelegate,
BPHomebrewManagerDelegate,
BPToolbarProtocol,
NSMenuDelegate,
NSOpenSavePanelDelegate>
```

Its `#pragma mark` sections show what has accumulated: footer label, homebrew-manager delegate, search mode, table-view delegate, two more delegates, menu delegate, **IBActions (lines 875–1365 — 490 lines on its own)**, and open/save panel delegate.

It is the junction for the sidebar, the table, the detail pane, search, the toolbar, the Dock menu, Brewfile import, reload progress, cancel, and every user operation. Recent work made this worse rather than better — the Dock menu (#133), Brewfile import (#136), reload progress (#138) and the reload Stop control (#139) each added another responsibility to this one file.

It also has **no direct test coverage**. It is the largest source file in the project and the only one of that size that nothing exercises directly:

| File | Lines | Covered |
|---|---|---|
| `BPHomebrewViewController.m` | 1374 | no |
| `BPHomebrewInterface.m` | 997 | yes |
| `BPSideBarController.m` | 610 | yes |
| `BPHomebrewManager.m` | 560 | yes |

The reason nothing tests it is circular: it is not in the `CakebrewTests` target, because pulling it in drags the whole UI object graph along. So its logic is only reachable through ~8-minute UI journeys.

## Proposal

Extract along the seams the `#pragma mark` sections already suggest, in separate thin slices — not one big move:

- **Operations** (install / uninstall / upgrade / pin / tap / cleanup / import / export confirmations and dispatch) into a coordinator that owns the confirmation sheets and the operation window.
- **Search** (`BPTimedDispatch` coalescing, restore-row-on-clear) into its own controller.
- **Reload presentation** (`didPublishListForMode:`, `didBeginStepForMode:`, reveal, empty state) into a presenter.
- Leave the view controller owning the view hierarchy and delegate plumbing.

Each extracted piece becomes unit-testable, which is the actual payoff.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `BPHomebrewViewController.m` is meaningfully smaller and no longer the junction for unrelated features
- [ ] At least one extracted collaborator is in the `CakebrewTests` target with direct tests
- [ ] Every existing UI journey still passes — this is behaviour-preserving
- [ ] Each extraction is its own PR

## Notes

This is a behaviour-changing refactor only in structure, so per AGENTS.md the tests come first: characterise the behaviour being moved with a test against the *new* seam, watch it fail, then move the code. The 41 UI journeys are the safety net for the parts that cannot be unit-tested — run them on every slice, not just the last.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

cd /Users/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/cakebrew
gh issue create --repo scottdensmore/Cakebrew \
  --title "The formula list ignores the keyboard: no Delete, no Return, no double-click" \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

The formula table responds to nothing but selection. `grep -rn "keyDown\|deleteBackward\|NSDeleteCharacter\|doubleAction" Cakebrew --include="*.m"` returns **no matches**.

So on a Mac app in 2026:

- **Delete** on a selected installed formula does nothing. Uninstall is only reachable from the toolbar or the context menu.
- **Return** does nothing. There is no default action for a row.
- **Double-clicking a row** does nothing — not install, not show info.

Every one of those is a standard AppKit idiom, and the actions they would map to already exist (`uninstallFormula:`, `installFormula:`, `showFormulaInfo:`). Multi-selection is already supported (`selectedRowIndexes`, `formulasAtIndexSet:`), so the keyboard path would inherit it.

This is the kind of gap that makes an app feel unfinished even when every feature is present: the mouse works, and the keyboard is dead.

## Proposal

- **Delete** → uninstall the selection, through the existing confirmation sheet. Enabled only when the selection is uninstallable in the current list.
- **Return** → the primary action for the current list: install in All Formulae / All Casks, upgrade in Outdated, show info in Installed.
- **Double-click** → same as Return.
- No action at all in the Tools lists (Doctor, Update, Services) and Repositories, where the concepts do not apply.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Unit test covers the row-action mapping — list mode + selection → action, including the modes that must map to nothing
- [ ] Delete on an installed formula opens the existing uninstall confirmation; cancelling runs no brew command
- [ ] Nothing happens for a selection that has no valid action, rather than the wrong thing happening
- [ ] Multi-selection behaves the same as the toolbar path

## Notes

The mapping is the testable seam and should be a pure function of (list mode, selection) → selector, in the same shape as `BPDockMenu +controllerActionForItem:`. Keyboard focus itself is **not** testable on CI — the headless runner's window is never key (AGENTS.md, "five ways a green local UI run lies"). So unit-test the mapping and verify the key handling by hand under `-BPMockBrew`.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -1

## Problem

README.md, under Installing:

> Download the latest build from [Releases](https://github.com/scottdensmore/Cakebrew/releases). Builds are signed with a Developer ID certificate, notarized and stapled, so they open without a Gatekeeper warning.

`gh release list` for this repo returns **nothing**. There has never been a release. Every claim in that paragraph is currently aspirational, and the only way to run the app is to build it from source.

This is the largest remaining gap between what the project says it is and what a user can actually get, and it is worth stating plainly: all the polish work is invisible to anyone who is not a developer.

## Why it has not happened

`.github/workflows/release.yml` is complete and triggers on a `v*` tag. It cannot run because it needs credentials that do not exist yet:

- a **Developer ID Application** certificate — separate from the Apple Development certificate, and the one thing that cannot be worked around
- repo secrets: `MACOS_CERTIFICATE_P12`, `MACOS_CERTIFICATE_PWD`, `KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`, `NOTARY_APPLE_ID`

AGENTS.md already records the certificate dependency under "Distribution & sandboxing". This issue exists so it is visible in the backlog rather than only in a doc.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A Developer ID Application certificate exists in the account and is exported for CI
- [ ] The five secrets are set on the repository
- [ ] A `v*` tag produces a signed, notarized, stapled build attached to a GitHub release
- [ ] The artifact is verified on a machine that has never built the app: it opens with no Gatekeeper warning, and the privileged helper registers
- [ ] README's Installing section is true

## Notes

Maintainer-blocked — the certificate is an Apple Developer account action nobody else can take.

Once releases exist, the natural follow-on is telling users about them: the app has **no update mechanism at all** (`grep -rn "Sparkle\|SUUpdater\|checkForUpdates"` → no matches), so someone who installs a build has no way to learn a newer one shipped. Both done. Here's where things landed.

## The workflow — [#141](https://github.com/scottdensmore/Cakebrew/pull/141)

`workflow.md` is deleted and AGENTS.md is now genuinely the single source of truth. **I didn't start over**, though you offered it. Most of AGENTS.md is accumulated measurement — the sandbox table, the five ways a green local UI run lies, the helper signing rules — and deleting that would have thrown away the expensive part. What was flat and partly stale was the *workflow*, so that's what I replaced.

What's actually new rather than reworded:

- **Phase 0 spikes** — absent before. Two decisions here were settled by measuring the opposite of the documented guess (the sandbox, and the `actool` icon probe), so the phase cites both as the pattern.
- **Inspect before mutating**, naming the real hazard: the live `.claude/`, `.codex/`, `.entire/` modifications this machine carries, which cost me time repeatedly this session.
- **Release builds required.** I checked before writing the rule — Release is clean (0 warnings, 18s) and CI has built it all along; only the local commands omitted it.
- **Prove the test bites.** Writing test and code together and never seeing red isn't TDD; mutation testing is the fallback, and the PR must say which was done. I did exactly this for `BPBrewfile` and it fell out as a rule.
- **Conventional Commits** going forward, history left alone. This commit is the first one.
- Four principles, each grounded in something concrete rather than stated abstractly.

Two corrections surfaced while rewriting: the testing section still described the `elementBoundByIndex:` disambiguation #134 removed, and the mock's opt-in flags were undocumented. CONTRIBUTING.md no longer restates the workflow; the PR template follows the new phases.

## The analysis — four issues filed

- **[#142](https://github.com/scottdensmore/Cakebrew/issues/142)** — **a third of the UI is untranslated.** 34–45 multi-word English sentences sit verbatim in each non-English locale, out of 184 keys, while the README advertises six localizations. This is a direct consequence of the English-placeholder rule working as designed with nothing ever converting placeholders into translations. `BPLocalizationParityTests` can't see it by construction.
- **[#143](https://github.com/scottdensmore/Cakebrew/issues/143)** — **`BPHomebrewViewController` is 1374 lines, 62 methods, 7 protocols**, with a 490-line IBActions section and no direct test coverage. Four of the features I shipped this session added to it.
- **[#144](https://github.com/scottdensmore/Cakebrew/issues/144)** — **the formula table ignores the keyboard entirely.** No Delete, no Return, no double-click; the actions all already exist.
- **[#145](https://github.com/scottdensmore/Cakebrew/issues/145)** — **the README points users at an empty Releases page.** Zero releases have ever been cut.

One candidate I dropped rather than filed: I suspected window state wasn't persisted, checked, and found `frameAutosaveName="MainWindow"` already in the xib. Not a finding.
